STRONGLY COMMUTING INTERVAL MAPS
ANA ANUˇSI´C AND CHRISTOPHER MOURON
Abstract. Maps f, g : I →I are called strongly commuting if f ◦g−1 = g−1 ◦f. We
show that strongly commuting, piecewise monotone maps f, g can be decomposed into
a ﬁnite number of invariant intervals (or period 2 intervals) on which f, g are either
both open maps, or at least one of them is monotone. As a consequence, we show that
strongly commuting piecewise monotone interval maps have a common ﬁxed point.
Results of the paper also have implications in understanding dynamical properties of
certain maps on inverse limit spaces.
1. Introduction
We assume that X is a topological space, often a continuum, i.e. a compact, connected,
metric space.
A continuous function f : X →X will be called a map.
Two maps
f, g : X →X are said to commute if f(g(x)) = g(f(x)) for all x ∈X. The concept
of commutativity is very basic, yet there still seems to be a surprising lack of tools for
understanding it, even when the space X is very simple, e.g. the unit interval I = [0, 1].
The research of commuting interval maps dates back to 1923, when Ritt gave a char-
acterization of commuting polynomials [21]. He showed that commuting polynomials
are ±xn, ±xn, for natural numbers n, m, Tchebychev polynomials, or iterates of the
same polynomial. The great advancement in the ﬁeld happened in the 50s and 60s, re-
lated to the question on the existence of a common ﬁxed point of commutating interval
maps. According to Baxter [3], the question was raised independently by Dyer in 1954,
Shields in 1955, and Dubins in 1956, and in higher generality by Isbell [13]. Precisely,
the question was whether for any two commuting maps f, g : I →I there exists x ∈I
such that f(x) = g(x) = x. For example, Ritt’s polynomials all have such property.
The question was settled in the negative independently by Boyce [6] and Huneke [12] in
1967. Detailed overview of the common ﬁxed point problem was given by McDowell in
[16]. Modern-day research asks about the existence of other common periodic points of
commuting interval maps (see e.g. [1], [8]), or assumes X is a more complicated space,
e.g. a square I2 (see [11],[15]), or an arc-like continuum (see [5], [19]). Overview of
other contemporary research in the area can be found in [7].

In this paper we give a partial answer to the following question (see also Question 2 in
[16]):
Question. What conditions on commuting maps f, g : I →I guarantee the existence
of a common ﬁxed point?
For example, Cohen shows in [9] that if f, g are open commuting maps, then they have
a common ﬁxed point. More generally, Joichi [14] and Folkman [10] show that it is
enough for only one of f, g to be open.
We introduce a notion of strongly commuting maps. We say that f, g : X →X are
strongly commuting if f(g−1(x)) = g−1(f(x)) for every x ∈X. Note that f and g
commute if and only if f(g−1(x)) ⊆g−1(f(x)) for every x ∈X, see Lemma 2.1. So
strongly commuting maps are indeed commuting.
Our motivation comes from the

maps turned out to have a very important role.

2. Preliminaries
Given two topological spaces X, Y , a continuous function f : X →Y will be referred to
as a map. We will restrict paper to compact, connected, metrizable spaces (also called
continua), and usually the unit interval I = [0, 1].
Set-valued function from X to Y is a function F : X →2Y , where 2Y denotes the set
of all non-empty closed subsets of Y . We always assume that set-valued functions are
upper semi-continuous, i.e., the graph of F,
Γ(F) = {(x, y) : y ∈F(x)}
is closed in X × Y . When there is no confusion, we will often abuse the notation and
denote set-valued functions as F : X →Y . By π1 : Γ(F) →X and π2 : Γ(F) →Y we
denote the projections to the ﬁrst and second coordinate.
We say that maps f, g : X →X commute if f(g(x)) = g(f(x)) for every x ∈X.
Lemma 2.1. Maps f : X →X and g : X →X commute if and only if f ◦g−1(x) ⊆
g−1 ◦f(x), for every x ∈X.
Proof. Note that f ◦g−1(x) = {f(y) : g(y) = x} and g−1 ◦f(x) = {z : g(z) = f(x)}.
So, given w = f(y) ∈f ◦g−1(x), we have g(f(y)) = f(g(y)) = f(x). It follows that
w ∈g−1 ◦f(x).
For the other direction, assume that f ◦g−1(x) ⊆g−1 ◦f(x), for every x ∈X. Take
any y ∈I and let g(y) = z. Then, since f(y) ∈f ◦g−1(z) ⊆g−1 ◦f(z), we have
g ◦f(y) = f(z) = f ◦g(y).
□
In particular, for commutative maps f, g : X →X, it holds that Γ(f ◦g−1) ⊆Γ(g−1◦f).
Remark 2.2. Note that
Γ(f ◦g−1) = {(g(t), f(t)) : t ∈X},
so the graph of f ◦g−1 can be parametrized by X. In particular, the graph of f ◦g−1
is connected. Furthermore, Γ(f ◦g−1) is closed in I2.
We say that f, g : X →X are strongly commuting if f ◦g−1(x) = g−1 ◦f(x) for all
x ∈X. Thus strongly commuting maps are commuting, but not vice-versa; see the
examples in the following section.
In what follows, we will restrict our functions and set-valued functions to X = I = [0, 1],
the unit interval. Let f : I →I be a map. We say that c ∈(0, 1) is a critical point of
f if f|U is not one-to-one for every open interval U ∋c. The set of critical points of f
will be denoted by Cf. We say that f is piecewise monotone if Cf is ﬁnite. We say that

4. Hats and endpoints
In this section we study the graphs of set-valued maps f ◦g−1 and g−1◦f. We introduce
the notions of hats and endpoints and then show that, when f and g strongly commute,
they exactly correspond to critical points of f.
Note that f −1 ◦g = g ◦f −1 if and only if g−1 ◦f = f ◦g−1, so in all of the results f
and g can be interchanged and the results are still true. For simplicity, the notions and
properties of hats and endpoints will be introduced for the set-valued map g−1 ◦f.

connected component of f −1(J) which contains x, and by V the connected component
of g−1(J) which contains y. We can assume that U ∩Cf = {x}, and V ∩Cg = ∅. Then
obviously U and V are open intervals in I, and g|V : V →J is a homeomorphism.
Let O = U × V , then O is an open disc in I2 and (x, y) ∈O.
Note that A :=
O ∩Γ(g−1 ◦f) = {(t, g−1(f(t)) ∩V ) : t ∈U}. Furthermore, we claim that ϕ: U →A

A can be parametrized by U, so it is an open arc which contains (x, y).

Assume that there is no t ∈T such that t ∈(0, 1). In that case T ⊂{0, 1}. Since (x, y)

Assume there is t ∈(0, 1) such that t ∈T. By Lemma 4.2, f(t) = y and y is an
extremum of π2(A), so there is a small neighbourhood U of t such that f(t′) < f(t) for

□
Remark 4.5. Let (x, y) ∈Γ(g−1 ◦f) be a hat, so it is contained in the interior of an
arc A ⊂Γ(g−1 ◦f) by Lemma 4.2. If g−1 ◦f = f ◦g−1, then Lemma 4.4 implies that
we can ﬁnd t = t(x, y) ∈Cf such that (x, y) = (g(t), f(t)), or (x, y) = (g(0), f(0)) =
(g(1), f(1)). Thus every hat corresponds to at least one critical point of f, or to the set

Abstract: Maps f, g : I →I are called strongly commuting if f ◦g−1 = g−1 ◦f. We show that strongly commuting, piecewise monotone maps f, g can be decomposed into a ﬁnite number of invariant intervals (or period 2 intervals) on which f, g are either both open maps, or at least one of them is monotone. As a consequence, we show that strongly commuting piecewise monotone interval maps have a common ﬁxed point. Results of the paper also have implications in understanding dynamical properties of certain maps on inverse limit spaces.
